summary: Explains the long-standing tradition of Independent Submissions, RFCs that do not come out of the IETF standards process. Such documents serve useful functions for the wider community, and this memo describes how people can submit them to the RFC Editor and how they are reviewed and published.

plainLanguage.summary: Independent Submissions are RFCs that do not come through the IETF standards process. RFC 4846 explains why they are published and how the RFC Editor receives, reviews, and decides on them. It gives the IESG a limited role in identifying conflicts with IETF work while leaving the final publication decision to the RFC Editor.

questions: how to submit an independent rfc
who decides whether an independent submission is published
what does the iesg review for independent submissions
subtitle: How the RFC Editor receives, reviews, and publishes documents outside the IETF standards process.

tldr.problem: The RFC Series includes documents that do not come from the IETF standards process, but their independent submission and review practices needed explanation.
tldr.mechanism: Authors submit an Internet-Draft to the RFC Editor, who arranges reviews and asks the IESG to check for conflicts with IETF work before making the publication decision.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes a process intended to preserve the independence of these submissions. It was later updated by RFC 5744.

today: RFC 4846 is an Informational RFC from July 2007 and has been updated by RFC 5744. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Independent Submissions in the RFC Series
sections.content:
The RFC Series predates the IETF and has long included documents outside the IETF standards process. RFC 4846 calls these Independent Submissions and describes editorial and processing norms for them.

The memo distinguishes Independent Submissions from documents produced by formal IETF, IAB, or IRTF groups, and from individual submissions that go to the IESG under Area Director sponsorship. It argues that independent publication is valuable because it keeps the RFC Series open to work beyond the IETF agenda.
sections.plainLanguage: Not every RFC is produced by an IETF working group. This memo explains the separate route for authors who submit work directly to the RFC Editor.

sections.title: What Independent Submissions Are For
sections.content:
Independent Submissions can discuss technologies outside the IETF agenda, introduce ideas from research, describe vendor-specific protocols or experience, and publish critiques of IETF standards proposals. The RFC also lists meeting reports, editorials, satire, eulogies, and technical contributions.

The memo treats critiques of alternatives to IETF standards as an important check on the standards process. A submission that conflicts with or offers an alternative to an IETF standard or proposal must clearly describe that relationship.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC Series can carry useful documents that do not belong to the IETF standards process. Keeping that route open also allows authors to publish critiques and alternatives.

sections.title: Submitting and Reviewing a Document
sections.content:
Authors first post a document as an Internet-Draft and then ask the RFC Editor to consider it for publication. The request should identify prior community discussion and the desired category, Informational or Experimental. The RFC Editor performs an initial check, arranges one or more reviews, and sends the authors a written summary.

Authors may respond to reviews or request additional reviews. The IAB may review a document in exceptional circumstances, but is not required to do so. The RFC Editor can reject a submission that does not meet the technical or editorial standards of the RFC Series, and the final publication decision rests with the RFC Editor.
sections.plainLanguage: Authors submit a draft and receive review comments from readers chosen by the RFC Editor. Authors can respond or ask for more reviews, but the RFC Editor makes the final publication decision.

sections.title: The IESG Conflict Review
sections.content:
Before a final decision, the RFC Editor normally sends the document to the IESG for a relatively short review. This is not a technical review. It focuses on possible conflicts or confusion with IETF processes and working-group activity.

The IESG may suggest explanatory text or request a delay. Under the agreement described in this RFC, a delay can be up to six months and may be renewed twice, for a total of 18 months. The IESG can request that a document not be published, but the RFC Editor considers the request and retains the final decision.
sections.plainLanguage: The IESG checks whether publication could conflict with IETF work. It can ask for a delay or explain a concern, but the RFC Editor decides whether to publish.

sections.title: Editorial Board and Review Transparency
sections.content:
The RFC Editor appoints and maintains the Editorial Review Board, which advises on submissions and review policy. The RFC Editor may ask the IAB for suggestions but keeps the final appointment decision to protect independence.

Authors receive reviews, normally with reviewer names unless a reviewer requests anonymity. After an accept or reject decision, the RFC Editor may publish the reviews and rebuttals. An author who objects to publication of reviews must generally act within 14 days of notice.
sections.plainLanguage: An editorial board advises the RFC Editor, who remains responsible for the process. Reviews are shared with authors and may later be made public, with anonymity available when requested.

sections.title: Rights and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC includes contribution rights so Independent Submission terms appear in one place. Contributors grant publication and distribution rights for drafts and RFCs, and grant rights for translations and certain derivative works under the stated conditions.

The Security Considerations section says the document describes an administrative publication procedure and has no specific security implications.
sections.plainLanguage: Submitting a document grants the stated rights to publish and distribute it. The RFC says its administrative process has no specific security implications.
